This paper reviews recent developments in deep neural networks for image, video, and geometric understanding, with emphasis on both performance and computational efficiency. We discuss convolutional, recurrent, residual, attention-based, generative, and graph-based architectures, as well as methods for transfer learning, semi-supervised learning, weak supervision, noisy labels, and unsupervised domain adaptation. Applications covered include image and video compression, restoration, synthesis, recognition, detection, segmentation, tracking, depth and 3D perception, face analysis, medical imaging, biological imaging, and agricultural and wildlife monitoring. We also examine approaches for learning compact representations, hashing, model compression, sparsification, efficient convolution, and deployment on resource-constrained platforms. Particular attention is given to the use of temporal, geometric, multimodal, and contextual information, together with strategies for interpretability, privacy preservation, and robustness to adversarial perturbations. By organizing these methods according to their learning objectives and visual tasks, the paper highlights common design principles, summarizes empirical progress, identifies current limitations, and outlines promising directions for developing accurate, efficient, and reliable vision systems.

original_abstract: Generating formal-language represented by relational tuples, such as Lisp programs or mathematical expressions, from a natural-language input is an extremely challenging task because it requires to explicitly capture discrete symbolic structural information from the input to generate the output. Most state-of-the-art neural sequence models do not explicitly capture such structure information, and thus do not perform well on these tasks. In this paper, we propose a new encoder-decoder model based on Tensor Product Representations (TPRs) for Natural- to Formal-language generation, called TP-N2F. The encoder of TP-N2F employs TPR 'binding' to encode natural-language symbolic structure in vector space and the decoder uses TPR 'unbinding' to generate a sequence of relational tuples, each consisting of a relation (or operation) and a number of arguments, in symbolic space. TP-N2F considerably outperforms LSTM-based Seq2Seq models, creating a new state of the art results on two benchmarks: the MathQA dataset for math problem solving, and the AlgoList dataset for program synthesis. Ablation studies show that improvements are mainly attributed to the use of TPRs in both the encoder and decoder to explicitly capture relational structure information for symbolic reasoning.
generated_abstract: This paper presents a systematic review of neural approaches for natural language understanding and generation, focusing on how learned representations are combined with linguistic structure, external knowledge, and multimodal evidence. We organize recent methods across question answering, dialogue, relation and sequence extraction, sentiment analysis, semantic parsing, machine translation, grammar induction, and text-to-image generation. Particular attention is given to graph neural networks for structured knowledge representations, recurrent and semi-Markov models for label and segment dependencies, multi-scale attention for long sequences, and compositional architectures that separate lexical and syntactic information. We also examine techniques for learning with limited or noisy supervision, including adversarial domain adaptation, distant supervision, abductive self-training, and grounding speech in visual context. Beyond predictive accuracy, we discuss interpretability, abstention, robustness to recognition and domain errors, and the reliability of automatic evaluation metrics. The review highlights recurring challenges: inadequate modeling of global dependencies, weak coordination among local decisions, limited transfer across languages and domains, and insufficiently meaningful evaluation. We conclude by outlining directions toward more data-efficient, interpretable, multilingual, and linguistically informed neural systems.

original_abstract: Using different sources of information to support automated extracting of relations between biomedical concepts contributes to the development of our understanding of biological systems. The primary comprehensive source of these relations is biomedical literature. Several relation extraction approaches have been proposed to identify relations between concepts in biomedical literature, namely using neural networks algorithms. The use of multichannel architectures composed of multiple data representations, as in deep neural networks, is leading to state-of-the-art results. The right combination of data representations can eventually lead us to even higher evaluation scores in relation extraction tasks. Thus, biomedical ontologies play a fundamental role by providing semantic and ancestry information about an entity. The incorporation of biomedical ontologies has already been proved to enhance previous state-of-the-art results.

This paper presents a broad review of contemporary methods for understanding and generating language across speech recognition, segmentation, classification, information extraction, dialogue, summarization, question answering, semantic parsing, and text generation. We organize existing approaches according to the linguistic structure they model, ranging from characters and words to sentences, documents, events, and heterogeneous knowledge graphs. Particular attention is given to methods that address limited supervision, feature sparsity, out-of-vocabulary words, domain shift, multilinguality, and the need for interpretable predictions. We also discuss strategies for incorporating document layout, discourse structure, external knowledge, human feedback, and synthetic or weak supervision into end-to-end systems. Across tasks, neural models often improve benchmark performance, but their errors reveal persistent difficulties with compositionality, commonsense reasoning, factuality, pragmatics, and robustness to noise and bias. The review concludes by identifying promising directions for explainable, data-efficient, socially responsible, and linguistically informed NLP systems, supported by reproducible datasets and evaluation protocols.

original_abstract: RDMA is an exciting technology that enables a host to access the memory of a remote host without involving the remote CPU. Prior work shows how to use RDMA to improve the performance of distributed in-memory storage systems. However, RDMA is widely believed to have scalability issues, due to the amount of active protocol state that needs to be cached in the limited NIC cache. These concerns led to several software-based proposals to enhance scalability by trading off performance. In this work, we revisit these trade-offs in light of newer RDMA hardware and propose new guidelines for scaling RDMA. We show that using one-sided remote memory primitives leads to higher performance compared to send/receive and kernel-based systems in rack-scale environments. Based on these insights, we design and implement Storm, a transactional dataplane using one-sided read and write-based RPC primitives. We show that Storm outperforms eRPC, FaRM, and LITE by 3.3x, 3.6x, and 17.1x, respectively, on an Infinband EDR cluster with Mellanox ConnectX-4 NICs.
generated_abstract: We present a scalable framework for dependable distributed computing across heterogeneous CPUs, GPUs, and dynamically changing networked resources. The framework combines performance-portable kernel execution with adaptive scheduling, allowing applications ranging from tensor contractions and deep-learning training to large scientific simulations and graph analytics to use diverse hardware without platform-specific redesign. To improve efficiency, the runtime exploits data layouts, batched linear-algebra kernels, approximate arithmetic, and lightweight contention management, while dynamically adapting synchronization and resource allocation to workload behavior and hardware variability. A fault-aware execution layer limits the cost of transient errors by relating recovery effort to application-level accuracy, and supports replicated tasks and transactional updates when stronger consistency is required. The system also accommodates elastic and adversarial environments through topology-aware communication and decentralized resource management. We evaluate the framework using representative numerical, machine-learning, sensing, and scientific workloads on heterogeneous clusters. Results show substantial reductions in execution time and synchronization overhead compared with conventional centralized or strictly synchronous approaches, while preserving configurable accuracy and consistency guarantees. These results demonstrate that combining adaptive coordination with portable low-level optimization can provide an effective foundation for efficient, resilient distributed applications.

original_abstract: Recent advances in language representation using neural networks have made it viable to transfer the learned internal states of a trained model to downstream natural language processing tasks, such as named entity recognition (NER) and question answering. It has been shown that the leverage of pre-trained language models improves the overall performance on many tasks and is highly beneficial when labeled data is scarce. In this work, we employ a pre-trained BERT with Conditional Random Fields (CRF) architecture to the NER task on the Portuguese language, combining the transfer capabilities of BERT with the structured predictions of CRF. We explore feature-based and fine-tuning training strategies for the BERT model. Our fine-tuning approach obtains new state-of-the-art results on the HAREM I dataset, improving the F1-score by 3.2 points on the selective scenario (5 NE classes) and by 3.8 points on the total scenario (10 NE classes).
generated_abstract: This paper presents a systematic overview of neural methods for natural language processing, focusing on how representations, linguistic structure, and available resources affect performance across tasks. We examine the transition from manually engineered features and fixed lexical vocabularies to distributed, contextual, character- and subword-level representations. The review covers language identification, named entity recognition, sentiment and emotion analysis, semantic similarity, discourse and argument parsing, coreference resolution, text complexity assessment, authorship analysis, recommendation, and machine translation. Particular attention is given to mechanisms that incorporate document context, discourse relations, morphology, word boundaries, coverage, and structural metadata, as well as to approaches that improve efficiency through parameter factorization and unsupervised adaptation. We compare the benefits and limitations of increasingly large corpora and neural architectures, noting that additional data and model capacity do not uniformly produce better linguistic generalization. Finally, we discuss dataset construction, transfer learning, evaluation practices, and the gap between benchmark performance and human-like understanding. The analysis suggests that robust progress depends on combining scalable representation learning with explicit structural knowledge, carefully designed resources, and evaluations that test generalization beyond the training distribution.

original_abstract: Decentralized solutions to finite-sum minimization are of significant importance in many signal processing, control, and machine learning applications. In such settings, the data is distributed over a network of arbitrarily-connected nodes and raw data sharing is prohibitive often due to communication or privacy constraints. In this article, we review decentralized stochastic first-order optimization methods and illustrate some recent improvements based on gradient tracking and variance reduction, focusing particularly on smooth and strongly-convex objective functions. We provide intuitive illustrations of the main technical ideas as well as applications of the algorithms in the context of decentralized training of machine learning models.
generated_abstract: Machine learning is evolving rapidly through the integration of deep architectures, probabilistic modeling, optimization, privacy, robustness, and interactive decision making. This paper presents a broad review of recent advances across supervised, unsupervised, semi-supervised, and reinforcement learning. We organize contemporary approaches according to their central methodological challenges: learning from limited, distributed, noisy, or selectively observed data; exploiting graphs, temporal structure, side information, and multimodal representations; adapting models online; and improving computational efficiency and interpretability. Particular attention is given to scalable neural architectures, representation learning, generative models, anomaly detection, recommendation, clustering, causality, and model-based reinforcement learning. We also examine practical concerns including adversarial and false-data attacks, differential privacy, Byzantine workers, uncertainty estimation, and the preservation of knowledge during adaptation or distillation. Alongside theoretical guarantees for convergence, regret, generalization, and privacy, we summarize empirical evidence from applications in medicine, science, language, vision, industrial maintenance, and multi-agent systems. The review highlights common trade-offs between accuracy, robustness, efficiency, and data requirements, and identifies promising directions toward reliable, flexible, and resource-aware learning systems capable of operating in dynamic real-world environments.

original_abstract: Modern text-to-speech (TTS) systems are able to generate audio that sounds almost as natural as human speech. However, the bar of developing high-quality TTS systems remains high since a sizable set of studio-quality   pairs is usually required. Compared to commercial data used to develop state-of-the-art systems, publicly available data are usually worse in terms of both quality and size. Audio generated by TTS systems trained on publicly available data tends to not only sound less natural, but also exhibits more background noise. In this work, we aim to lower TTS systems' reliance on high-quality data by providing them the textual knowledge extracted by deep pre-trained language models during training. In particular, we investigate the use of BERT to assist the training of Tacotron-2, a state of the art TTS consisting of an encoder and an attention-based decoder. BERT representations learned from large amounts of unlabeled text data are shown to contain very rich semantic and syntactic information about the input text, and have potential to be leveraged by a TTS system to compensate the lack of high-quality data. We incorporate BERT as a parallel branch to the Tacotron-2 encoder with its own attention head. For an input text, it is simultaneously passed into BERT and the Tacotron-2 encoder. The representations extracted by the two branches are concatenated and then fed to the decoder. As a preliminary study, although we have not found incorporating BERT into Tacotron-2 generates more natural or cleaner speech at a human-perceivable level, we observe improvements in other aspects such as the model is being significantly better at knowing when to stop decoding such that there is much less babbling at the end of the synthesized audio and faster convergence during training.

This paper surveys recent advances in neural methods for language understanding, generation, and structured prediction. We review word embeddings, contextual representations, recurrent and convolutional networks, attention mechanisms, memory and reinforcement-learning approaches, and emerging transformer-based models. Their applications are examined across text classification, sentiment and emotion analysis, discourse and anaphora resolution, information extraction, grammatical error modeling, machine translation, reading comprehension, dialogue, summarization, poetry generation, and language-guided robotics. We also discuss multimodal and multilingual learning, weak and low-resource supervision, model compression, quantization, and the use of external lexical and commonsense resources. Particular attention is given to the relationship between representation quality, architectural complexity, interpretability, and generalization across domains and languages. Through comparison of reported results and methodological choices, the paper identifies recurring strengths and limitations of current approaches, including data dependence, computational cost, opacity, and difficulty with long-range reasoning and linguistic variation. We conclude by outlining research directions involving more efficient, explainable, transferable, and linguistically informed neural language systems.

original_abstract: We present Location Field Descriptors, a novel approach for single image 3D model retrieval in the wild. In contrast to previous methods that directly map 3D models and RGB images to an embedding space, we establish a common low-level representation in the form of location fields from which we compute pose invariant 3D shape descriptors. Location fields encode correspondences between 2D pixels and 3D surface coordinates and, thus, explicitly capture 3D shape and 3D pose information without appearance variations which are irrelevant for the task. This early fusion of 3D models and RGB images results in three main advantages: First, the bottleneck location field prediction acts as a regularizer during training. Second, major parts of the system benefit from training on a virtually infinite amount of synthetic data. Finally, the predicted location fields are visually interpretable and unblackbox the system. We evaluate our proposed approach on three challenging real-world datasets (Pix3D, Comp, and Stanford) with different object categories and significantly outperform the state-of-the-art by up to 20% absolute in multiple 3D retrieval metrics.

We examine convolutional, recurrent, adversarial, metric-learning, attention-based, and graph-based models, together with emerging strategies for weakly supervised, semi-supervised, zero-shot, few-shot, and self-supervised learning. Particular attention is given to practical challenges, including long-tailed distributions, noisy web annotations, occlusion, domain and modality shifts, adverse illumination, computational constraints, and adversarial manipulation. We also discuss applications involving hyperspectral and infrared imagery, medical imaging, remote sensing, autonomous navigation, and human–computer interaction. Comparative analysis of representative datasets and evaluation protocols highlights the importance of robust features, temporal and geometric reasoning, multimodal fusion, and efficient deployment. Finally, we identify open problems in interpretability, data efficiency, security, generalization, and reliable real-world operation.

original_abstract: Rotation detection is a challenging task due to the difficulties of locating the multi-angle objects and separating them accurately and quickly from the background. Though considerable progress has been made, there still exist challenges for rotating objects with large aspect ratio, dense distribution and category extremely imbalance. In this paper, we propose an end-to-end refined single-stage rotation detector for fast and accurate positioning objects. Considering the shortcoming of feature misalignment in the current refined single-stage detector, we design a feature refinement module to improve detection performance, which is especially effective in the long tail data set. The key idea of feature refinement module is to re-encode the position information of the current refined bounding box to the corresponding feature points through feature interpolation to realize feature reconstruction and alignment. Extensive experiments on two remote sensing public datasets DOTA, HRSC2016 as well as scene text data ICDAR2015 show the state-of-the-art accuracy and speed of our detector. Source code and the models will be made public available upon the publish of the paper.

This paper reviews recent advances in deep learning for visual understanding, with emphasis on convolutional, recurrent, residual, graph-based, generative, and nonparametric architectures. We organize existing methods according to their representation, learning strategy, supervision level, and computational requirements, covering recognition, detection, segmentation, tracking, retrieval, pose and action analysis, three-dimensional reconstruction, and image generation. We also examine applications in autonomous driving, surveillance, biometrics, medical imaging, remote sensing, robotics, and artistic analysis. Particular attention is given to learning under limited or weak supervision, domain shift, multimodal inputs, uncertainty estimation, adversarial robustness, model interpretability, and efficient deployment on embedded hardware. Across these settings, we compare the advantages of end-to-end learning with approaches that incorporate geometric models, graphs, temporal structure, hand-crafted priors, or external knowledge. Finally, we identify persistent challenges, including data and annotation scarcity, generalization across environments, computational cost, reliability in safety-critical applications, and the lack of standardized evaluation protocols. The review highlights promising directions toward more adaptable, explainable, efficient, and trustworthy visual intelligence.

original_abstract: Existing conversational systems tend to generate generic responses. Recently, Background Based Conversations (BBCs) have been introduced to address this issue. Here, the generated responses are grounded in some background information. The proposed methods for BBCs are able to generate more informative responses, they either cannot generate natural responses or have difficulty in locating the right background information. In this paper, we propose a Reference-aware Network (RefNet) to address the two issues. Unlike existing methods that generate responses token by token, RefNet incorporates a novel reference decoder that provides an alternative way to learn to directly cite a semantic unit (e.g., a span containing complete semantic information) from the background. Experimental results show that RefNet significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods in terms of both automatic and human evaluations, indicating that RefNet can generate more appropriate and human-like responses.
generated_abstract: Natural language processing systems increasingly rely on large annotated datasets, yet annotation remains costly, domain-dependent, and difficult to scale, particularly for specialized and low-resource languages. This paper presents a systematic study of active learning for NLP, examining how annotation strategies, model uncertainty, representation quality, and task structure affect learning efficiency. We unify active-learning experiments across diverse tasks, including named-entity recognition, grammatical error detection, sentiment analysis, relation extraction, question answering, and document classification, using both traditional and pretrained neural models. We compare random sampling with uncertainty-, disagreement-, diversity-, and hybrid-based acquisition methods, and analyze performance at multiple annotation budgets. Our results show that active learning can substantially reduce the amount of labeled data required, but its benefits vary with task complexity, class imbalance, domain shift, and the calibration of the underlying model. Strategies based on richer uncertainty estimates generally outperform confidence-only selection, while diversity safeguards against redundant or misleading batches. We further discuss annotation noise, transfer learning, and evaluation practices, and provide recommendations for deploying active-learning pipelines in practical NLP settings. The study identifies open challenges and establishes directions for more robust, reproducible, and resource-efficient language technology development.

original_abstract: Cryptocurrencies have garnered much attention in recent years, both from the academic community and industry. One interesting aspect of cryptocurrencies is their explicit consideration of incentives at the protocol level. Understanding how to incorporate this into the models used to design cryptocurrencies has motivated a large body of work, yet many open problems still exist and current systems rarely deal with incentive related problems well. This issue arises due to the gap between Cryptography and Distributed Systems security, which deals with traditional security problems that ignore the explicit consideration of incentives, and Game Theory, which deals best with situations involving incentives. With this work, we aim to offer a systematization of the work that relates to this problem, considering papers that blend Game Theory with Cryptography or Distributed systems and discussing how they can be related. This gives an overview of the available tools, and we look at their (potential) use in practice, in the context of existing blockchain based systems that have been proposed or implemented.
generated_abstract: The rapid expansion of connected devices, cloud services, intelligent applications, and decentralized infrastructures has created a complex and constantly evolving cybersecurity landscape. This paper presents a multidisciplinary survey of recent advances in cyber defense, emphasizing how modern security mechanisms address threats across software, hardware, networks, mobile systems, vehicles, and blockchain platforms. We organize existing work into several themes: machine-learning-based detection and adversarial robustness; privacy-preserving authentication, communication, and data analysis; side-channel and speculative-execution defenses; secure cloud and mobile execution; resilient vehicular and Internet-of-Things systems; and trustworthy blockchain, voting, and certificate infrastructures. For each theme, we compare security objectives, attacker capabilities, deployment assumptions, computational costs, and empirical validation practices. We also examine recurring limitations, including dependence on trusted authorities, inadequate protection against adaptive attackers, privacy–utility and security–performance trade-offs, scalability constraints, and gaps between formal guarantees and real-world implementations. Finally, we identify open challenges involving composable security, explainable and continuously adaptive defenses, standard evaluation methodologies, and practical integration across heterogeneous platforms. The study provides a structured foundation for researchers and practitioners developing robust, privacy-preserving, and deployable cybersecurity solutions.

original_abstract: Language models have become a key step to achieve state-of-the art results in many different Natural Language Processing (NLP) tasks. Leveraging the huge amount of unlabeled texts nowadays available, they provide an efficient way to pre-train continuous word representations that can be fine-tuned for a downstream task, along with their contextualization at the sentence level. This has been widely demonstrated for English using contextualized representations (Dai and Le, 2015; Peters et al., 2018; Howard and Ruder, 2018; Radford et al., 2018; Devlin et al., 2019; Yang et al., 2019b). In this paper, we introduce and share FlauBERT, a model learned on a very large and heterogeneous French corpus. Models of different sizes are trained using the new CNRS (French National Centre for Scientific Research) Jean Zay supercomputer. We apply our French language models to diverse NLP tasks (text classification, paraphrasing, natural language inference, parsing, word sense disambiguation) and show that most of the time they outperform other pre-training approaches. Different versions of FlauBERT as well as a unified evaluation protocol for the downstream tasks, called FLUE (French Language Understanding Evaluation), are shared to the research community for further reproducible experiments in French NLP.
generated_abstract: We present a neural framework for developing emotionally aware conversational agents that can recognize users’ needs and generate appropriate, informative, and empathetic responses. The proposed system combines contextual language representations with sentiment, emotion, and aspect information, while modeling dialogue history and latent conversational intentions. To improve robustness in realistic settings, we incorporate character-level representations for noisy and morphologically diverse text, transfer learning from large question-answering and language-modeling resources, and mechanisms for handling named entities and code-switched utterances. We further investigate multimodal signals, including visual context, for conversations involving personal experiences and mental health. The model is evaluated on goal-oriented and open-domain dialogue data, as well as social-media posts requiring empathy, and is compared with recurrent, convolutional, and transformer-based baselines. Automatic measures show improvements in response relevance, emotion consistency, and contextual coherence, while human judgments indicate that generated responses are more empathetic, engaging, and linguistically natural. Ablation studies demonstrate that explicit emotion modeling and dialogue context are especially important for multi-turn interactions. The results highlight the value of combining semantic understanding, affective reasoning, and transfer learning in practical conversational systems.

original_abstract: The use of background knowledge remains largely unexploited in many text classification tasks. We propose tax2vec, a parallel algorithm for constructing taxonomy based features, and demonstrate its use on six short-text classification problems, including gender, age and personality type prediction, drug effectiveness and side effect prediction, and news topic prediction. The experimental results indicate that the interpretable features constructed using tax2vec can notably improve the performance of classifiers; the constructed features, in combination with fast, linear classifiers tested against strong baselines, such as hierarchical attention neural networks, achieved comparable or better classification results on short documents. Further, tax2vec can also serve for extraction of corpus-specific keywords. Finally, we investigated the semantic space of potential features where we observe a similarity with the well known Zipf's law.

original_abstract: High storage and computational costs obstruct deep neural networks to be deployed on resource-constrained devices. However, most existing methods on knowledge distillation ignore the valuable information among training process associated with training results. In this paper, we provide a new Collaborative Teaching Knowledge Distillation (CTKD) strategy which employs two special teachers. Specifically, one teacher trained from scratch (i.e., scratch teacher) assists the student step by step using its temporary outputs. It forces the student to approach the optimal path towards the final logits with high accuracy. The other pre-trained teacher (i.e., expert teacher) guides the student to focus on a critical region which is more useful for the task. The combination of the knowledge from two special teachers can significantly improve the performance of the student network in knowledge distillation. The results of experiments on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, SVHN and Tiny ImageNet datasets verify that the proposed knowledge distillation method is efficient and achieves state-of-the-art performance.

original_abstract: This work investigates if the current neural architectures are adequate for learning symbolic rewriting. Two kinds of data sets are proposed for this research -- one based on automated proofs and the other being a synthetic set of polynomial terms. The experiments with use of the current neural machine translation models are performed and its results are discussed. Ideas for extending this line of research are proposed and its relevance is motivated.

original_abstract: Polygonal meshes provide an efficient representation for 3D shapes. They explicitly captureboth shape surface and topology, and leverage non-uniformity to represent large flat regions as well as sharp, intricate features. This non-uniformity and irregularity, however, inhibits mesh analysis efforts using neural networks that combine convolution and pooling operations. In this paper, we utilize the unique properties of the mesh for a direct analysis of 3D shapes using MeshCNN, a convolutional neural network designed specifically for triangular meshes. Analogous to classic CNNs, MeshCNN combines specialized convolution and pooling layers that operate on the mesh edges, by leveraging their intrinsic geodesic connections. Convolutions are applied on edges and the four edges of their incident triangles, and pooling is applied via an edge collapse operation that retains surface topology, thereby, generating new mesh connectivity for the subsequent convolutions. MeshCNN learns which edges to collapse, thus forming a task-driven process where the network exposes and expands the important features while discarding the redundant ones. We demonstrate the effectiveness of MeshCNN on various learning tasks applied to 3D meshes.

The study also identifies key trade-offs among expressiveness, interpretability, privacy, communication, and safety, providing practical guidelines for deploying learning systems in dynamic real-world environments.

original_abstract: Zero-shot learning (ZSL) has received extensive attention recently especially in areas of fine-grained object recognition, retrieval, and image captioning. Recent work also showed adversarially robust generalization requires more data. This may significantly affect the robustness of ZSL. However, very few efforts have been devoted towards this direction. In this paper, we take an initial attempt, and propose a generic formulation to provide a systematical solution (named ATZSL) for learning a robust ZSL model. It is capable of achieving better generalization on various adversarial objects recognition while only losing a negligible performance on clean images for unseen classes, by casting ZSL into a min-max optimization problem. To address it, we design a defensive relation prediction network, which can bridge the seen and unseen class domains via attributes to generalize prediction and defense strategy. Additionally, our framework can be extended to deal with the poisoned scenario of unseen class attributes. An extensive group of experiments are then presented, demonstrating that ATZSL obtains remarkably more favorable trade-off between model transferability and robustness, over currently available alternatives under various settings.

original_abstract: We present a target-driven navigation approach for improving the cross-target and cross-scene generalization for visual navigation. Our approach incorporates an information-theoretic regularization into a deep reinforcement learning (RL) framework. First, we present a supervised generative model to constrain the intermediate process of the RL policy, which is used to generate a future observation from a current observation and a target. Next, we predict a navigation action by analyzing the difference between the generated future and the current. Our approach takes into account the connection between current observations and targets, and the interrelation between actions and visual transformations. This results in a compact and generalizable navigation model. We perform experiments on the AI2-THOR framework and the Active Vision Dataset (AVD) and show at least 7.8% improvement in navigation success rate and 5.7% in SPL, compared to the supervised baseline, in unexplored environments.

original_abstract: Quizbowl is a scholastic trivia competition that tests human knowledge and intelligence; additionally, it supports diverse research in question answering (QA). A Quizbowl question consists of multiple sentences whose clues are arranged by difficulty (from obscure to obvious) and uniquely identify a well-known entity such as those found on Wikipedia. Since players can answer the question at any time, an elite player (human or machine) demonstrates its superiority by answering correctly given as few clues as possible. We make two key contributions to machine learning research through Quizbowl: (1) collecting and curating a large factoid QA dataset and an accompanying gameplay dataset, and (2) developing a computational approach to playing Quizbowl that involves determining both what to answer and when to answer. Our Quizbowl system has defeated some of the best trivia players in the world over a multi-year series of exhibition matches. Throughout this paper, we show that collaborations with the vibrant Quizbowl community have contributed to the high quality of our dataset, led to new research directions, and doubled as an exciting way to engage the public with research in machine learning and natural language processing.

The review highlights a consistent movement from task-specific architectures toward adaptable systems that combine pretrained representations with structured and contextual reasoning. We conclude by identifying open directions for building NLP systems that are more data-efficient, transparent, robust, socially responsible, and capable of reasoning over language in realistic environments.

original_abstract: Contextual word representations, typically trained on unstructured, unlabeled text, do not contain any explicit grounding to real world entities and are often unable to remember facts about those entities. We propose a general method to embed multiple knowledge bases (KBs) into large scale models, and thereby enhance their representations with structured, human-curated knowledge. For each KB, we first use an integrated entity linker to retrieve relevant entity embeddings, then update contextual word representations via a form of word-to-entity attention. In contrast to previous approaches, the entity linkers and self-supervised language modeling objective are jointly trained end-to-end in a multitask setting that combines a small amount of entity linking supervision with a large amount of raw text. After integrating WordNet and a subset of Wikipedia into BERT, the knowledge enhanced BERT (KnowBert) demonstrates improved perplexity, ability to recall facts as measured in a probing task and downstream performance on relationship extraction, entity typing, and word sense disambiguation. KnowBert's runtime is comparable to BERT's and it scales to large KBs.

We organize prior work according to the representations and learning strategies employed, including contextual and domain-adapted embeddings, attention and recurrent models, structured prediction, knowledge graphs, weak and multilingual supervision, transfer learning, and federated or resource-efficient training. We further examine applications involving clinical text, social media, political claims, endangered languages, and speech. Across these settings, we identify recurring benefits from contextual modeling, explicit structure, adaptive data selection, and joint learning, while highlighting limitations caused by spurious correlations, annotation scarcity, computational cost, and biased representations. The review concludes with research directions for reliable, interpretable, multilingual, and socially responsible language technologies.

original_abstract: Retrieve-and-edit based approaches to structured prediction, where structures associated with retrieved neighbors are edited to form new structures, have recently attracted increased interest. However, much recent work merely conditions on retrieved structures (e.g., in a sequence-to-sequence framework), rather than explicitly manipulating them. We show we can perform accurate sequence labeling by explicitly (and only) copying labels from retrieved neighbors. Moreover, because this copying is label-agnostic, we can achieve impressive performance in zero-shot sequence-labeling tasks. We additionally consider a dynamic programming approach to sequence labeling in the presence of retrieved neighbors, which allows for controlling the number of distinct (copied) segments used to form a prediction, and leads to both more interpretable and accurate predictions.
generated_abstract: Natural language processing has advanced rapidly through the development of neural architectures, large-scale datasets, and increasingly general representations of language. We review recurrent, convolutional, capsule, transformer, tree-based, and structured prediction models, emphasizing how attention, multitask learning, reinforcement learning, transfer learning, and ensemble methods improve robustness and generalization. Particular attention is given to multilingual and low-resource settings, noisy social media and health-related text, conversational context, and applications in education and political analysis. We also discuss resources and evaluation practices, including benchmark construction for Indonesian summarization, speech commands, semantic role labeling, and realistic online reviews. Across these areas, progress is substantial, but challenges remain in data scarcity, domain adaptation, interpretability, factuality, evaluation, and the handling of long-range discourse and pragmatic context. The survey concludes by outlining opportunities for models that integrate linguistic structure, world knowledge, multimodal evidence, and human-centered objectives.

original_abstract: Selecting in-domain data from a large pool of diverse and out-of-domain data is a non-trivial problem. In most cases simply using all of the available data will lead to sub-optimal and in some cases even worse performance compared to carefully selecting a matching set. This is true even for data-inefficient neural models. Acoustic Latent Dirichlet Allocation (aLDA) is shown to be useful in a variety of speech technology related tasks, including domain adaptation of acoustic models for automatic speech recognition and entity labeling for information retrieval. In this paper we propose to use aLDA as a data similarity criterion in a data selection framework. Given a large pool of out-of-domain and potentially mismatched data, the task is to select the best-matching training data to a set of representative utterances sampled from a target domain. Our target data consists of around 32 hours of meeting data (both far-field and close-talk) and the pool contains 2k hours of meeting, talks, voice search, dictation, command-and-control, audio books, lectures, generic media and telephony speech data. The proposed technique for training data selection, significantly outperforms random selection, posterior-based selection as well as using all of the available data.
generated_abstract: We present a context-aware, semi-supervised framework for lifelong sentiment classification in Modern Standard Arabic and Egyptian Arabic. Linguistically motivated resources are incorporated, including sentiment lexicons, idioms, intensifiers, shifters, negation patterns, and syntactic indicators of conflicting expressions. A semantic analysis component provides interpretable representations of lexical and compositional meaning while avoiding computationally intractable assumptions about possible worlds. During training, the system extracts sentiment-bearing words, contextual patterns, and domain-independent knowledge from previously processed tasks and reuses them when learning from new, partially labeled data. Experiments on Arabic tweets, hotel reviews, and product-related microblogs show that the proposed model consistently outperforms conventional supervised and unsupervised baselines, including Naive Bayes, standard recurrent networks, and static vector similarity methods. The results demonstrate that combining contextual modeling, fuzzy semantic composition, and lifelong knowledge transfer improves robustness across domains, dialects, and evolving sentiment vocabularies.

original_abstract: With advancements in deep model architectures, tasks in computer vision can reach optimal convergence provided proper data preprocessing and model parameter initialization. However, training on datasets with low feature-richness for complex applications limit and detriment optimal convergence below human performance. In past works, researchers have provided external sources of complementary data at the cost of supplementary hardware, which are fed in streams to counteract this limitation and boost performance. We propose a generative multi-stream architecture, eliminating the need for additional hardware with the intent to improve feature richness without risking impracticability. We also introduce the compact spatio-temporal residual block to the standard 3-dimensional convolutional model, C3D. Our rC3D model performs comparatively to the top C3D residual variant architecture, the pseudo-3D model, on the FASL-RGB dataset. Our methods have achieved 95.62% validation accuracy with a variance of 1.42% from training, outperforming past models by 0.45% in validation accuracy and 5.53% in variance.

Particular attention is given to the practical challenges that limit deployment, such as scarce or noisy annotations, domain shift, class imbalance, geometric constraints, computational cost, and the lack of interpretability. We compare representative datasets, evaluation protocols, and reported results, highlighting the advantages and limitations of current approaches. The review further discusses efficient batching and model compression, confidence estimation, and mechanisms for incorporating expert knowledge or auxiliary modalities. Finally, we identify open research directions toward robust, explainable, data-efficient, and computationally economical vision systems capable of reliable operation across clinical, biometric, autonomous, and real-world sensing applications.

original_abstract: We present a novel framework for machine translation evaluation using neural networks in a pairwise setting, where the goal is to select the better translation from a pair of hypotheses, given the reference translation. In this framework, lexical, syntactic and semantic information from the reference and the two hypotheses is compacted into relatively small distributed vector representations, and fed into a multi-layer neural network that models the interaction between each of the hypotheses and the reference, as well as between the two hypotheses. These compact representations are in turn based on word and sentence embeddings, which are learned using neural networks. The framework is flexible, allows for efficient learning and classification, and yields correlation with humans that rivals the state of the art.
generated_abstract: Natural language processing systems are often evaluated on in-domain test sets that do not reflect the variability, ambiguity, and noise encountered in real-world use. We organize evidence from a broad range of tasks, including machine translation, Chinese word segmentation, dialogue generation, information extraction, fact checking, semantic representation, and mental-health analysis. Across these settings, we find that strong aggregate scores frequently conceal substantial weaknesses on linguistically targeted or naturally occurring challenge cases. Simple changes to decoding, vocabulary selection, sampling, or training data can significantly alter performance, while domain-adaptive representations and synthetic perturbations often provide larger gains than architectural modifications. We further show that evaluation quality depends critically on annotation uncertainty, temporal and gradient phenomena, and the distinction between generation quality and diversity. Based on these findings, we propose an evaluation framework combining standard metrics with challenge sets, human judgments, calibration, and adversarial testing, and outline practical recommendations for developing NLP systems that are more reliable beyond their training distributions.

original_abstract: While deep learning is successful in a number of applications, it is not yet well understood theoretically. A satisfactory theoretical characterization of deep learning however, is beginning to emerge. It covers the following questions: 1) representation power of deep networks 2) optimization of the empirical risk 3) generalization properties of gradient descent techniques --- why the expected error does not suffer, despite the absence of explicit regularization, when the networks are overparametrized? In this review we discuss recent advances in the three areas. In approximation theory both shallow and deep networks have been shown to approximate any continuous functions on a bounded domain at the expense of an exponential number of parameters (exponential in the dimensionality of the function). However, for a subset of compositional functions, deep networks of the convolutional type can have a linear dependence on dimensionality, unlike shallow networks. In optimization we discuss the loss landscape for the exponential loss function and show that stochastic gradient descent will find with high probability the global minima. To address the question of generalization for classification tasks, we use classical uniform convergence results to justify minimizing a surrogate exponential-type loss function under a unit norm constraint on the weight matrix at each layer -- since the interesting variables for classification are the weight directions rather than the weights. Our approach, which is supported by several independent new results, offers a solution to the puzzle about generalization performance of deep overparametrized ReLU networks, uncovering the origin of the underlying hidden complexity control.
generated_abstract: Machine learning systems are increasingly deployed in settings that demand more than predictive accuracy: they must generalize beyond their training distribution, quantify uncertainty, remain robust to perturbations and hardware faults, and provide interpretable decisions under computational and data constraints. We organize the literature around four complementary themes: representation learning and transfer, reliable prediction and uncertainty estimation, efficient and scalable optimization, and structured reasoning over graphs, time, and physical systems. We examine approaches based on calibration, diverse ensembles, information bottlenecks, continuous-time dynamics, domain adaptation, symbolic constraints, and hierarchical policies, highlighting their assumptions and trade-offs. We further discuss applications in networking, robotics, biology, healthcare, education, cybersecurity, and recommender systems. The analysis emphasizes recurring challenges, including distribution shift, partial observability, biased data, reproducibility, and the tension between accuracy, interpretability, safety, and resource consumption. Finally, we identify promising directions for developing machine learning systems that combine data-driven flexibility with reliable uncertainty, structural prior knowledge, and verifiable behavior.

original_abstract: Recent studies have shown that deep neural networks (DNNs) are vulnerable to various attacks, including evasion attacks and poisoning attacks. On the defense side, there have been intensive interests in provable robustness against evasion attacks. In this paper, we focus on improving model robustness against more diverse threat models. Specifically, we provide the first unified framework using smoothing functional to certify the model robustness against general adversarial attacks. In particular, we propose the first robust training process RAB to certify against backdoor attacks. We theoretically prove the robustness bound for machine learning models based on the RAB training process, analyze the tightness of the robustness bound, as well as proposing different smoothing noise distributions such as Gaussian and Uniform distributions. Moreover, we evaluate the certified robustness of a family of "smoothed" DNNs which are trained in a differentially private fashion. In addition, we theoretically show that for simpler models such as K-nearest neighbor models, it is possible to train the robust smoothed models efficiently. For K=1, we propose an exact algorithm to smooth the training process, eliminating the need to sample from a noise distribution.Empirically, we conduct comprehensive experiments for different machine learning models such as DNNs, differentially private DNNs, and KNN models on MNIST, CIFAR-10 and ImageNet datasets to provide the first benchmark for certified robustness against backdoor attacks. In particular, we also evaluate KNN models on a spambase tabular dataset to demonstrate its advantages. Both the theoretic analysis for certified model robustness against arbitrary backdoors, and the comprehensive benchmark on diverse ML models and datasets would shed light on further robust learning strategies against training time or even general adversarial attacks on ML models.
generated_abstract: Machine learning is rapidly moving from isolated predictive models to large-scale, interactive systems that must learn from heterogeneous data, adapt to changing environments, and operate under strict computational, privacy, and reliability constraints. We also discuss emerging approaches for generative modeling, anomaly detection, architecture search, continual and meta-learning, and privacy-preserving inference. Across these areas, we identify recurring tensions between accuracy, scalability, interpretability, robustness, and resource consumption. Particular attention is given to evaluation methodology, reproducibility, and the gap between laboratory benchmarks and real-world operation. Finally, we outline open problems in trustworthy decision making, adaptation under distribution shift, efficient collaboration across devices and domains, and the development of unified machine learning infrastructures that can support dependable applications at scale.

original_abstract: Face detection has witnessed significant progress due to the advances of deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs). Its central issue in recent years is how to improve the detection performance of tiny faces. To this end, many recent works propose some specific strategies, redesign the architecture and introduce new loss functions for tiny object detection. In this report, we start from the popular one-stage RetinaNet approach and apply some recent tricks to obtain a high performance face detector. Specifically, we apply the Intersection over Union (IoU) loss function for regression, employ the two-step classification and regression for detection, revisit the data augmentation based on data-anchor-sampling for training, utilize the max-out operation for classification and use the multi-scale testing strategy for inference. As a consequence, the proposed face detection method achieves state-of-the-art performance on the most popular and challenging face detection benchmark WIDER FACE dataset.
generated_abstract: Deep learning has transformed computer vision by enabling systems to learn representations directly from images, videos, and three-dimensional data. Particular attention is given to methods that improve robustness to noise, occlusion, scale variation, limited supervision, domain shift, and unseen classes. We also discuss efficient inference for low-power and real-time systems, normalization and optimization for constrained training settings, multimodal and graph-based reasoning, and generative and adversarial models for prediction and data synthesis. Finally, we consider interpretability, self-supervised and weakly supervised learning, and the role of structured priors in reducing annotation requirements. The review highlights common design principles, summarizes empirical trends across benchmark datasets, and identifies open challenges concerning generalization, computational cost, reliable evaluation, and the development of vision systems capable of reasoning about complex physical and semantic environments.

original_abstract: Human beings are creatures of habit. In their daily life, people tend to repeatedly consume similar types of food items over several days and occasionally switch to consuming different types of items when the consumptions become overly monotonous. However, the novel and repeat consumption behaviors have not been studied in food recommendation research. More importantly, the ability to predict daily eating habits of individuals is crucial to improve the effectiveness of food recommender systems in facilitating healthy lifestyle change. In this study, we analyze the patterns of repeat food consumptions using large-scale consumption data from a popular online fitness community called MyFitnessPal (MFP), conduct an offline evaluation of various state-of-the-art algorithms in predicting the next-day food consumption, and analyze their performance across different demographic groups and contexts. The experiment results show that algorithms incorporating the exploration-and-exploitation and temporal dynamics are more effective in the next-day recommendation task than most state-of-the-art algorithms.
generated_abstract: We present a scalable framework for discovering, representing, and recommending real-world events from heterogeneous Web data. To improve robustness, corroborative physical sources can be combined with noisy social streams, while controversy, sentiment, and confirmation bias are modeled to characterize competing perspectives and avoid overly narrow information exposure. Events and entities are organized in a heterogeneous graph linking topics, locations, people, media, and user interactions. Path-constrained relatedness, learned neural representations, and approximate inner-product search support efficient retrieval at large scale. A neural ranking component combines document structure, subtopic-level matching, timeliness, novelty, and multimodal evidence. Personalized recommendations are generated from implicit feedback and sequential behavior, with knowledge-aware negative sampling used to improve training under sparse observations and cold-start conditions. Experiments on large news, social-media, and recommendation collections show that the framework improves event detection, retrieval relevance, diversity, and recommendation accuracy over conventional content-based and collaborative baselines, while remaining suitable for real-time deployment.

original_abstract: Federated learning (FL) rests on the notion of training a global model in a decentralized manner. Under this setting, mobile devices perform computations on their local data before uploading the required updates to improve the global model. However, when the participating clients implement an uncoordinated computation strategy, the difficulty is to handle the communication efficiency (i.e., the number of communications per iteration) while exchanging the model parameters during aggregation. Therefore, a key challenge in FL is how users participate to build a high-quality global model with communication efficiency. We tackle this issue by formulating a utility maximization problem, and propose a novel crowdsourcing framework to leverage FL that considers the communication efficiency during parameters exchange. First, we show an incentive-based interaction between the crowdsourcing platform and the participating client's independent strategies for training a global learning model, where each side maximizes its own benefit. We formulate a two-stage Stackelberg game to analyze such scenario and find the game's equilibria. Second, we formalize an admission control scheme for participating clients to ensure a level of local accuracy. Simulated results demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed solution with up to 22% gain in the offered reward.
generated_abstract: Machine learning is rapidly expanding beyond conventional prediction tasks into systems that reason, adapt, generate, and make decisions under uncertainty. original_abstract: Specifying a complete domain model is time-consuming, which has been a bottleneck of AI planning technique application in many real-world scenarios. Most classical domain-model learning approaches output a domain model in the form of the declarative planning language, such as STRIPS or PDDL, and solve new planning instances by invoking an existing planner. However, planning in such a representation is sensitive to the accuracy of the learned domain model which probably cannot be used to solve real planning problems. In this paper, to represent domain models in a vectorization representation way, we propose a novel framework based on graph neural network (GNN) integrating model-free learning and model-based planning, called LP-GNN. By embedding propositions and actions in a graph, the latent relationship between them is explored to form a domain-specific heuristics. We evaluate our approach on five classical planning domains, comparing with the classical domain-model learner ARMS. The experimental results show that the domain models learned by our approach are much more effective on solving real planning problems.
generated_abstract: Modern autonomous systems must learn from heterogeneous, incomplete, and continuously changing information while making decisions under computational and perceptual constraints. The approach incorporates formal semantics for uncertain and nonmonotonic knowledge, scalable approximate inference, and temporal abstractions for cooperative multi-agent control. To make learning practical at scale, we consider external-memory models, mixed-precision training, and anytime algorithms that provide progressively improving solutions with explicit quality bounds. We further discuss knowledge extraction from large multimodal data collections, including audio-visual streams and formal contexts, and evaluate the framework in simulated and real-world scenarios involving robotic capability learning, event recognition, rescue coordination, and spectrum management. The results indicate that combining interpretable reasoning with adaptive learning improves robustness, data efficiency, and scalability, while exposing important challenges concerning theoretical guarantees, resource allocation, and the interaction between learned and symbolic components.

original_abstract: Statistical language modeling techniques have successfully been applied to source code, yielding a variety of new software development tools, such as tools for code suggestion and improving readability. A major issue with these techniques is that code introduces new vocabulary at a far higher rate than natural language, as new identifier names proliferate. But traditional language models limit the vocabulary to a fixed set of common words. For code, this strong assumption has been shown to have a significant negative effect on predictive performance. But the open vocabulary version of the neural network language models for code have not been introduced in the literature. We present a new open-vocabulary neural language model for code that is not limited to a fixed vocabulary of identifier names. We employ a segmentation into subword units, subsequences of tokens chosen based on a compression criterion, following previous work in machine translation. Our network achieves best in class performance, outperforming even the state-of-the-art methods of Hellendoorn and Devanbu that are designed specifically to model code. Furthermore, we present a simple method for dynamically adapting the model to a new test project, resulting in increased performance. We showcase our methodology on code corpora in three different languages of over a billion tokens each, hundreds of times larger than in previous work. To our knowledge, this is the largest neural language model for code that has been reported.
generated_abstract: Modern software systems are increasingly distributed, adaptive, data-intensive, and assembled from reusable components, making dependable development difficult. The studies also show that effectiveness depends strongly on context, data quality, human expertise, and the explainability of automated recommendations. original_abstract: This paper contributes to the challenge of learning a function on streamed multimodal data through evaluation. The core of the result of our paper is the combination of two quite different approaches to this problem. One comes from the mathematically principled technology of signatures and log-signatures as representations for streamed data, while the other draws on the techniques of recurrent neural networks (RNN). The ability of the former to manage high sample rate streams and the latter to manage large scale nonlinear interactions allows hybrid algorithms that are easy to code, quicker to train, and of lower complexity for a given accuracy. #R##N#We illustrate the approach by approximating the unknown functional as a controlled differential equation. Linear functionals on solutions of controlled differential equations are the natural universal class of functions on data streams. Following this approach, we propose a hybrid Logsig-RNN algorithm that learns functionals on streamed data. By testing on various datasets, i.e. synthetic data, NTU RGB+D 120 skeletal action data, and Chalearn2013 gesture data, our algorithm achieves the outstanding accuracy with superior efficiency and robustness.
generated_abstract: Machine learning is increasingly applied to problems involving structured data, sequential decisions, complex scientific models, and sensitive information. We further examine reinforcement learning, imitation learning, bandit algorithms, active learning, surrogate optimization, and hierarchical control for decision-making under limited or delayed feedback. Particular attention is given to scalable training through minibatch sampling, variance reduction, adaptive schedules, and data-efficient architecture search. Finally, we review approaches addressing privacy, fairness, interpretability, uncertainty, catastrophic forgetting, and formal safety guarantees. Across these areas, the evidence shows that successful learning systems increasingly combine data-driven models with structural priors, domain knowledge, and principled uncertainty or constraint handling. The paper identifies common challenges, including robustness to distribution shift, sample efficiency, reliable evaluation, and transfer to real-world settings, and outlines directions for developing more efficient, transparent, and dependable machine learning systems.

original_abstract: Low bit-width integer weights and activations are very important for efficient inference, especially with respect to lower power consumption. We propose Monte Carlo methods to quantize the weights and activations of pre-trained neural networks without any re-training. By performing importance sampling we obtain quantized low bit-width integer values from full-precision weights and activations. The precision, sparsity, and complexity are easily configurable by the amount of sampling performed. Our approach, called Monte Carlo Quantization (MCQ), is linear in both time and space, with the resulting quantized, sparse networks showing minimal accuracy loss when compared to the original full-precision networks. Our method either outperforms or achieves competitive results on multiple benchmarks compared to previous quantization methods that do require additional training.
generated_abstract: Machine learning is evolving from a collection of task-specific algorithms into a broad framework for learning representations, decisions, and structures from heterogeneous data. We further discuss learning under limited supervision, including curriculum learning, imitation learning, active learning, collaborative filtering, and model selection. Particular attention is given to sequential decision making, multi-agent coordination, continuous control, and adaptation under noisy or changing observations. Finally, we examine practical and societal requirements, including uncertainty quantification, fairness, privacy-preserving deletion, robustness to poisoned data and memory faults, sim-to-real transfer, and efficient hardware implementation. Across these areas, we identify recurring challenges involving generalization, computational scalability, interpretability, and reliable deployment. The paper organizes existing results into a unified perspective and outlines directions toward adaptive learning systems that can continuously integrate data, manage uncertainty, and operate safely in complex environments.

original_abstract: Many recent works demonstrated that Deep Learning models are vulnerable to adversarial examples.Fortunately, generating adversarial examples usually requires white-box access to the victim model, and the attacker can only access the APIs opened by cloud platforms. Thus, keeping models in the cloud can usually give a (false) sense of security.Unfortunately, cloud-based image classification service is not robust to simple transformations such as Gaussian Noise, Salt-and-Pepper Noise, Rotation and Monochromatization. In this paper,(1) we propose one novel attack method called Image Fusion(IF) attack, which achieve a high bypass rate,can be implemented only with OpenCV and is difficult to defend; and (2) we make the first attempt to conduct an extensive empirical study of Simple Transformation (ST) attacks against real-world cloud-based classification services. Through evaluations on four popular cloud platforms including Amazon, Google, Microsoft, Clarifai, we demonstrate that ST attack has a success rate of approximately 100% except Amazon approximately 50%, IF attack have a success rate over 98% among different classification services. (3) We discuss the possible defenses to address these security challenges.Experiments show that our defense technology can effectively defend known ST attacks.
generated_abstract: Deep learning has transformed computer vision by enabling end-to-end learning of representations for recognition, reconstruction, segmentation, registration, and multimodal perception. This paper reviews recent advances in deep neural methods across a broad range of visual tasks, emphasizing how architectural design, training strategies, and auxiliary information address persistent challenges. We examine recurrent and attention-based models for active recognition, video understanding, compression, and narrative generation; encoder-decoder and refinement networks for dense semantic labeling; and three-dimensional architectures for surface reconstruction, pulmonary nodule detection, pose estimation, and medical image registration. We also discuss methods for face recognition under disguise and surgical alteration, few-shot classification, referring-expression segmentation, colorization, makeup transfer, and visual navigation. Particular attention is given to efficiency and deployment, including quantization, low-power inference, real-time mapping, and learning from incomplete or unlabeled data. Finally, we consider robustness and fairness, highlighting hard-example mining, propagation-based data augmentation, permutation-invariant multimodal learning, and adversarial mitigation of gender bias. The review identifies common principles underlying these approaches and outlines open problems involving generalization, interpretability, annotation costs, computational constraints, and responsible use of visual learning systems.

original_abstract: Classical approaches for one-class problems such as one-class SVM (Scholkopf et al., 1999) and isolation forest (Liu et al., 2008) require careful feature engineering when applied to structured domains like images. To alleviate this concern, state-of-the-art methods like DeepSVDD (Ruff et al., 2018) consider the natural alternative of minimizing a classical one-class loss applied to the learned final layer representations. However, such an approach suffers from the fundamental drawback that a representation that simply collapses all the inputs minimizes the one class loss; heuristics to mitigate collapsed representations provide limited benefits. In this work, we propose Deep Robust One Class Classification (DROCC) method that is robust to such a collapse by training the network to distinguish the training points from their perturbations, generated adversarially. DROCC is motivated by the assumption that the interesting class lies on a locally linear low dimensional manifold. Empirical evaluation demonstrates DROCC's effectiveness on two different one-class problem settings and on a range of real-world datasets across different domains - images(CIFAR and ImageNet), audio and timeseries, offering up to 20% increase in accuracy over the state-of-the-art in anomaly detection.
generated_abstract: Machine learning systems are increasingly deployed in settings where data are limited, distributions change, decisions are sequential, and predictions must satisfy physical, computational, or societal constraints. We organize the literature around four complementary challenges: learning useful representations, exploiting unlabeled or streaming data, making decisions through interaction, and incorporating structure and prior knowledge. We discuss methods including manifold-based distances, semi-supervised and few-shot learning, continual learning, active search, Bayesian and reinforcement-learning policies, neural architecture and sequence-model optimization, and theory-guided models for scientific and engineering applications. Across these areas, we emphasize that benchmark performance alone is insufficient: representations influence task complexity, optimal behavior should remain invariant across related tasks, and deployment requires attention to bias, robustness, latency, memory, and safety. We further examine applications in healthcare, environmental monitoring, drug discovery, networking, and physical-system control. The synthesis identifies common principles for improving generalization and sample efficiency, highlights unresolved theoretical and practical limitations, and proposes directions for evaluating machine-learning methods in realistic, resource-constrained, and distribution-shifting environments.

original_abstract: Gaze correction aims to redirect the person's gaze into the camera by manipulating the eye region, and it can be considered as a specific image resynthesis problem. Gaze correction has a wide range of applications in real life, such as taking a picture with staring at the camera. In this paper, we propose a novel method that is based on the inpainting model to learn from the face image to fill in the missing eye regions with new contents representing corrected eye gaze. Moreover, our model does not require the training dataset labeled with the specific head pose and eye angle information, thus, the training data is easy to collect. To retain the identity information of the eye region in the original input, we propose a self-guided pretrained model to learn the angle-invariance feature. Experiments show our model achieves very compelling gaze-corrected results in the wild dataset which is collected from the website and will be introduced in details. Code is available at this https URL.
generated_abstract: Deep learning has transformed computer vision by enabling systems to learn increasingly useful representations directly from images, video, depth, audio, and other sensory data. This paper reviews recent advances in learning-based visual analysis and synthesis, with emphasis on convolutional, residual, recurrent, adversarial, and autoencoding architectures. We examine their application to image restoration, super-resolution, geometric correction, image retrieval, object detection, semantic segmentation, facial analysis, pose and action recognition, medical imaging, agricultural monitoring, and multimodal perception. Particular attention is given to methods that address limited supervision, missing or uncertain data, open-set recognition, domain shift, bias, and the need to preserve identity or semantic structure during generation. We also discuss computational strategies for practical deployment, including network pruning, efficient filtering, patch-distance computation, and FPGA-based acceleration. Across these areas, we compare the benefits and limitations of synthetic data, weak supervision, disentangled representations, recurrent memory, and adversarial objectives. The review concludes by identifying open challenges involving interpretability, reliability, fairness, realistic uncertainty modeling, data efficiency, and the deployment of accurate models on resource-constrained devices.

original_abstract: The lack of large-scale real datasets with annotationsmakes transfer learning a necessity for video activity under-standing. Within this scope, we aim at developing an effec-tive method for low-shot transfer learning for first-personaction classification. We leverage independently trained lo-cal visual cues to learn representations that can be trans-ferred from a source domain providing primitive action la-bels to a target domain with only a handful of examples.Such visual cues include object-object interactions, handgrasps and motion within regions that are a function of handlocations. We suggest a framework based on meta-learningto appropriately extract the distinctive and domain invari-ant components of the deployed visual cues, so to be able totransfer action classification models across public datasetscaptured with different scene configurations. We thoroughlyevaluate our methodology and report promising results overstate-of-the-art action classification approaches for bothinter-class and inter-dataset transfer.
generated_abstract: Deep learning has transformed computer vision by enabling systems to learn hierarchical representations directly from images, video, signals, and multimodal data.
